questions.prompt: Which detail is important when choosing an enum?
options: Enums can only represent numbers and never strings.
Enums can produce runtime output; a literal union is an alternative when only a compile-time set is needed.
Every enum is removed from emitted JavaScript in every configuration.
questions.answer_key: Enums can produce runtime output; a literal union is an alternative when only a compile-time set is needed.
questions.explanation: Consider runtime output and the intended contract when choosing enum or union alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Enums in TypeScript”?
options: The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
The concept should be demonstrated with numeric enums and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with numeric enums and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Numeric enums”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Enums in TypeScript”?
options: Check string enums, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
Assume enum runtime output and alternatives using unions is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
questions.answer_key: Check string enums, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “String enums”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
